questions.stem: A 68-year-old kidney transplant recipient hospitalized for pneumonia develops a painful vesicular rash confined to one band across the left trunk that does not cross the midline. Intravenous acyclovir is started. Which of the following best describes how this drug interferes with viral replication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks viral attachment by occupying the host cell surface receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: It competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate for incorporation into viral DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits viral neuraminidase and blocks release of newly formed virions

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and terminates the RNA chain

choices.label: E
choices.text: It inhibits viral thymidine kinase and prevents nucleoside phosphorylation

explanation.summary: Acyclovir is a guanosine analog that is incorporated into growing viral DNA and prevents strand lengthening.
explanation.whyCorrect: Guanosine analogs are guanosine (a purine) attached to a sugar, so their chemical structure mimics nucleosides. The activated triphosphate competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate for incorporation into the growing viral DNA strand, and once added it prevents further lengthening of that strand. The result is reduced viral DNA synthesis and reduced viral proliferation, which shortens the duration and severity of a reactivation such as this dermatomal zoster.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No antiherpetic drug in this class acts at receptor binding or viral entry; they all act at nucleic acid synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neuraminidase inhibition is the mechanism of oseltamivir, an influenza drug, and is not how any antiherpetic agent works.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting RNA-dependent RNA polymerase with chain termination describes sofosbuvir, used for hepatitis C, not acyclovir.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral thymidine kinase is the enzyme that activates acyclovir, not the enzyme acyclovir inhibits.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: Acyclovir and the other guanosine analogs have very little activity in uninfected human cells. Which of the following best explains this specificity for herpesviruses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human cells do not use the guanosine nucleotides that these drugs resemble

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are actively transported only into cells displaying viral surface antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are destroyed by human enzymes before they can reach the cell nucleus

choices.label: D
choices.text: They bind irreversibly to the viral capsid before the particle enters a cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: They must be phosphorylated by virus-specific kinases present in infected cells

explanation.summary: Guanosine analogs are specific for herpesviruses because viral kinases are required to activate them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir, and ganciclovir are prodrug-like nucleoside analogs that must be phosphorylated before they can be incorporated into DNA. That first phosphorylation is carried out by virus-specific enzymes such as thymidine kinase and UL97, which are present only where the virus is replicating. Drug is therefore activated preferentially inside infected cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Human cells use guanosine nucleotides constantly; that is precisely why these drugs are not perfectly selective.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Selectivity comes from intracellular activation, not from a transport system that recognizes viral antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The drugs are active in infected human cells, so host degradation cannot be the basis of their selectivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These agents act on DNA synthesis inside the cell and have no effect on the capsid of an extracellular virion.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with AIDS has perianal herpes simplex ulcers that continue to enlarge despite several weeks of oral acyclovir followed by valacyclovir. A viral isolate is confirmed to be drug resistant. Which of the following changes in the virus is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mutation in the host DNA polymerase gene that reduces drug binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mutation in the UL97 phosphotransferase gene carried by the virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: A mutation that results in decreased viral thymidine kinase activity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overproduction of viral DNA polymerase that outcompetes the drug

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of an efflux pump that exports drug from the infected cell

explanation.summary: Acyclovir resistance in herpes simplex is caused by mutations that lower viral thymidine kinase activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thymidine kinase phosphorylation is the first step in activating acyclovir and its relatives. A mutation that decreases thymidine kinase activity decreases the amount of active drug generated inside the infected cell, so the drug fails despite adequate dosing. Resistant herpesvirus strains are found primarily in immunosuppressed patients such as this one, where a persistently high viral load and chronic antiviral exposure give resistant strains the chance to emerge.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Resistance is a property of the virus; a host polymerase mutation is not a described mechanism of antiherpetic failure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: UL97 mutation is the resistance mechanism for ganciclovir in cytomegalovirus, not for acyclovir in herpes simplex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Resistance arises from failure to activate the drug, not from making more of the polymerase target.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Efflux pump upregulation is not a described mechanism of herpesvirus resistance to these agents.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: The patient described above has herpes simplex ulcers caused by a strain with markedly reduced thymidine kinase activity. Which of the following drugs is the most appropriate choice for his infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acyclovir

choices.label: B
choices.text: Famciclovir

choices.label: C
choices.text: Foscarnet

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penciclovir

choices.label: E
choices.text: Valacyclovir

explanation.summary: Foscarnet is the drug of choice for thymidine kinase-deficient, acyclovir-resistant herpes simplex.
explanation.whyCorrect: Foscarnet inhibits the viral DNA polymerase directly and does not need to be activated by a viral enzyme first. Because the resistance mechanism here is loss of the activating kinase, foscarnet bypasses the problem entirely and remains effective.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acyclovir is the drug that already failed; the thymidine kinase mutation is specifically resistance to it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Famciclovir is in the same family and shares the same activation step, so the mutation confers resistance to it as well.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Penciclovir also requires viral kinase activation and is only a topical agent for orolabial herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Valacyclovir is a prodrug of acyclovir and still depends on viral thymidine kinase for activation.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with AIDS is treated with foscarnet for a herpesvirus infection. Which of the following best characterizes this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A guanosine analog that terminates the chain after viral kinase activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A neuraminidase inhibitor that prevents budding of virions from the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: A nucleoside analog phosphorylated by host kinases to an active triphosphate

choices.label: D
choices.text: A protease inhibitor that blocks cleavage of viral polyprotein precursors

choices.label: E
choices.text: A pyrophosphate analog that noncompetitively inhibits viral polymerases

explanation.summary: Foscarnet is a pyrophosphate analog and a noncompetitive inhibitor of viral RNA and DNA polymerases.
explanation.whyCorrect: Foscarnet belongs to the viral DNA polymerase inhibitor class along with cidofovir. It is a pyrophosphate analog rather than a nucleoside analog, and it acts as a noncompetitive inhibitor of many viral RNA and DNA polymerases. Because it does not need phosphorylation by a viral enzyme, it works against strains that have lost their activating kinase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: That describes acyclovir and its relatives, which are nucleoside analogs activated by viral kinases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neuraminidase inhibition is an influenza drug mechanism and has no role against herpesviruses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Host kinase activation describes cidofovir; foscarnet is not a nucleoside analog and is not phosphorylated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No antiherpetic agent covered here acts as a protease inhibitor.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 55-year-old transplant recipient receiving intravenous ganciclovir for cytomegalovirus disease has a leukocyte count of 1,800/mm3, platelet count of 62,000/mm3, and hemoglobin of 8.4 g/dL. Which of the following adverse effects of this drug best accounts for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune hemolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow suppression

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate antagonism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron malabsorption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration

explanation.summary: Ganciclovir characteristically causes leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the antiherpetic drugs, ganciclovir is the one associated with myelosuppression. The expected pattern is exactly what this patient shows: a low white cell count, a low platelet count, and anemia. Blood counts must therefore be followed during ganciclovir therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ganciclovir is not described as a cause of immune-mediated red cell destruction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antiherpetic drugs are nucleoside and pyrophosphate analogs, not folate antagonists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired iron absorption would not explain the simultaneous drop in white cells and platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration is not a listed adverse effect of any antiherpetic agent.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man with AIDS begins foscarnet therapy. Two days later he reports perioral tingling and develops carpopedal spasm during blood pressure measurement. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities is most likely present?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypercalcemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hyperkalemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypernatremia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyperphosphatemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypocalcemia

explanation.summary: Foscarnet causes renal impairment together with electrolyte disturbances, notably hypocalcemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond renal impairment, foscarnet is specifically associated with electrolyte derangements including hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and hypomagnesemia. Perioral paresthesias and carpopedal spasm are the classic bedside signs of a low ionized calcium, so electrolytes should be checked and repleted during therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A high calcium level would not cause tetany; foscarnet lowers calcium rather than raising it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Foscarnet drives potassium down rather than up, so hypokalemia is the expected direction.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sodium excess is not among the electrolyte disturbances attributed to foscarnet.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Phosphate elevation is not a described foscarnet effect and would not produce these symptoms.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with severe disseminated herpes simplex infection is given high-dose intravenous acyclovir. Over the next 48 hours her serum creatinine rises from 0.8 mg/dL to 2.3 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains this change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct toxic injury to the renal artery endothelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drug-induced diuresis producing severe volume depletion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune complex glomerulonephritis triggered by the drug

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of both ureters by retroperitoneal fibrosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Precipitation of crystallized drug within the renal tubules

explanation.summary: Renal impairment from intravenous acyclovir and ganciclovir results from crystal nephropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Intravenous acyclovir and ganciclovir can crystallize and precipitate within the renal tubules, a process called crystal nephropathy, which produces an acute rise in creatinine. This is why proper hydration is maintained whenever these agents are given intravenously.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Renal arterial endothelial toxicity is not a described mechanism for these agents.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The injury comes from drug precipitating in the tubules, not from excessive urine output.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An immune complex mechanism is not how antiherpetic drugs injure the kidney.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These drugs do not cause retroperitoneal fibrosis or mechanical ureteral obstruction.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman admitted for intravenous acyclovir has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on hospital day 2, and there is erythema and tenderness along the vein used for infusion. Apart from renal impairment, which of the following additional findings fits this drug's adverse effect profile?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated serum aminotransferase levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Irreversible sensorineural hearing loss

choices.label: C
choices.text: Optic neuritis with loss of color vision

choices.label: D
choices.text: Severe neutropenia with thrombocytopenia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Symptomatic hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia

explanation.summary: Acyclovir is associated with increased liver enzymes, increased seizure risk, and phlebitis when given intravenously.
explanation.whyCorrect: The adverse effect list specific to acyclovir includes rising liver enzymes and an increased risk of seizures, plus vein irritation when the drug is infused. This patient shows the neurologic and local vascular effects, so an increase in aminotransferases is the expected accompanying laboratory abnormality.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hearing loss is not a described toxicity of acyclovir or any other agent in this group.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Optic neuritis is not among the adverse effects attributed to antiherpetic drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukopenia and thrombocytopenia belong to ganciclovir, not acyclovir.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Electrolyte disturbances of this kind are characteristic of foscarnet.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with frequent recurrences of genital herpes is prescribed valacyclovir instead of acyclovir and asks why. Which of the following is the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It acts on a different viral enzyme than acyclovir does

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can be applied topically as well as taken by mouth

choices.label: C
choices.text: It does not require activation by any viral kinase enzyme

choices.label: D
choices.text: It eliminates virus that lies dormant in the sensory neurons

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a prodrug of acyclovir with greater oral bioavailability

explanation.summary: Valacyclovir is a prodrug of acyclovir with better gastrointestinal absorption and bioavailability.
explanation.whyCorrect: A prodrug is metabolized into its active form within the host. Valacyclovir is converted to acyclovir after absorption, and it is absorbed from the gut better than acyclovir itself, so more active drug reaches the circulation from an oral dose. That pharmacokinetic advantage is the reason it is often chosen for oral therapy of recurrent outbreaks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Once converted, valacyclovir is acyclovir and acts by exactly the same mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Valacyclovir is an oral agent; penciclovir is the topical drug in this group.
whyWrongByChoice.C: As an acyclovir prodrug it still depends on viral kinase activation after conversion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No antiherpetic drug clears latent virus from neurons; these agents manage outbreaks but do not cure the infection.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A clinician is choosing among oral agents for an outbreak of orolabial herpes. Famciclovir differs from acyclovir chiefly in which of the following ways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It inhibits viral DNA polymerase without needing activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a prodrug with better gastrointestinal absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a pyrophosphate analog rather than a nucleoside analog

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is available only as an intravenous preparation

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is effective against cytomegalovirus but not against HSV-2

explanation.summary: Famciclovir is a prodrug whose advantage over acyclovir is better gastrointestinal absorption.
explanation.whyCorrect: Famciclovir and valacyclovir are the two prodrugs among the antiherpetic guanosine analogs, meaning they are metabolized into their active form within the host. Famciclovir's stated advantage is improved gastrointestinal absorption, which makes oral dosing more reliable than with acyclovir.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activation-independent polymerase inhibition describes foscarnet, not famciclovir.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Famciclovir is a guanosine analog; foscarnet is the pyrophosphate analog.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Famciclovir is an oral drug; acyclovir is the only agent in this class given both orally and intravenously.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Famciclovir is used for HSV-1, HSV-2, and varicella-zoster virus, not for cytomegalovirus.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man has recurrent mild cold sores on the vermilion border of the lip and prefers a cream to pills. Which of the following agents is used topically for this indication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cidofovir

choices.label: B
choices.text: Foscarnet

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ganciclovir

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penciclovir

choices.label: E
choices.text: Valganciclovir

explanation.summary: Penciclovir is the topical antiherpetic agent, and its use is limited to orolabial herpes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Localized herpes infection can be treated topically or orally, with topical therapy reserved for mild cases because it is less effective than oral therapy. Penciclovir is specifically the topical treatment for orolabial herpes only, which matches this patient's mild recurrent cold sores.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cidofovir is a parenteral drug used mainly for cytomegalovirus retinitis in patients with AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Foscarnet is given intravenously for herpesvirus infection in immunocompromised patients.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ganciclovir is an intravenous agent used for cytomegalovirus, not a topical cold sore treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Valganciclovir is the oral prodrug of ganciclovir and is used for cytomegalovirus.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 1 of 2: Drugs to Treat Herpesvirus Infections

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV infection is started on a regimen containing emtricitabine, a cytosine analogue. The drug competes with the individual nucleotides and is incorporated into the nucleotide chain that is being built as viral RNA is copied into DNA. Which of the following best describes how this drug stops viral replication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds gp41 after gp120 engages, preventing viral fusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds integrase, preventing insertion of DNA into the genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: It blocks protease, preventing cleavage into mature viral units

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits hepatic CYP450, raising levels of other antivirals

choices.label: E
choices.text: It terminates the growing DNA strand, halting reverse transcription

explanation.summary: Nucleotide/nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors are chain terminators that stop reverse transcriptase.
explanation.whyCorrect: NRTIs are analogues of adenosine (tenofovir), cytosine (emtricitabine, lamivudine), guanosine (abacavir), or thymidine (zidovudine). They compete with the natural nucleotides and are incorporated into the growing nucleotide chain, where they act as chain terminators and stop reverse transcriptase. Because retroviruses must convert RNA to DNA to replicate, this blockade halts the viral life cycle, which is why NRTIs are a mainstay of treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding gp41 once it is exposed by gp120 attachment is the mechanism of the fusion inhibitor enfuvirtide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking integrase is the mechanism of the integrase strand transfer inhibitors, not of a nucleoside analogue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking protease is how protease inhibitors stop budding of mature virions, a later step entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting hepatic CYP450 describes the pharmacokinetic enhancers ritonavir and cobicistat.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with HIV infection has efavirenz added to his regimen. Unlike the nucleoside analogues he is already taking, this drug is not incorporated into the elongating DNA strand; instead it attaches directly to a viral enzyme and inactivates it, so that the DNA strand being made is left incomplete and useless. Which enzyme is inactivated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatic cytochrome P450

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human DNA polymerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

explanation.summary: NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcriptase by binding directly to the enzyme rather than by chain termination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, like NRTIs, inhibit reverse transcriptase, but they do so by binding directly to the enzyme and inactivating it. This stops the DNA chain from polymerizing and leaves the elongating strand incomplete. NNRTIs such as efavirenz are often used together with NRTIs, especially tenofovir.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatic cytochrome P450 is a host enzyme targeted by boosters, not the viral enzyme inactivated here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Human DNA polymerase is a host enzyme whose inhibition explains NRTI mitochondrial toxicity, not the antiviral effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Integrase is the target of the integrase strand transfer inhibitors such as raltegravir and dolutegravir.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protease is the target of the protease inhibitors, which act at the final budding step.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with drug-resistant HIV infection is started on maraviroc. The drug prevents the virus from binding to a molecule on the surface of the host cell, so that the virus is unable to enter. Which of the following does this drug block?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CCR5

choices.label: B
choices.text: gp120

choices.label: C
choices.text: gp41

choices.label: D
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Protease

explanation.summary: Maraviroc is an entry inhibitor that blocks the host CCR5 coreceptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: For HIV to enter a host cell it must first bind a surface receptor and then fuse with the membrane. One of these receptors is CCR5. Maraviroc blocks CCR5, which prevents binding of the virus and leaves it unable to enter the cell. It is sometimes useful in patients with drug-resistant virus infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: gp120 is the viral envelope protein that attaches to the cell; maraviroc acts on the host coreceptor instead.
whyWrongByChoice.C: gp41 is the viral protein bound by enfuvirtide, which blocks fusion rather than receptor binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Integrase is the enzyme that inserts viral DNA into the host genome and is targeted by INSTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protease is an intracellular viral enzyme targeted by protease inhibitors, not by entry inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman with HIV infection is given enfuvirtide. The target of this drug is not accessible on free virions; it becomes exposed only after the virus has bound gp120 to the cell surface, and blocking it prevents the virus from fusing with the membrane and entering the cell. Which of the following is the target?

choices.label: A
choices.text: gp41

choices.label: B
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

choices.label: D
choices.text: The CCR5 coreceptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: The p17 matrix protein

explanation.summary: Enfuvirtide binds gp41, which is exposed once HIV binds through gp120, and blocks fusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Entry requires binding followed by fusion. Enfuvirtide binds gp41, a viral protein that becomes exposed once HIV binds gp120 to the cell surface. Binding gp41 blocks fusion of the virus with the membrane and therefore blocks its entry into the cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Integrase acts inside the cell after reverse transcription and is targeted by INSTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reverse transcriptase acts after entry and is targeted by NRTIs and NNRTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The CCR5 coreceptor is blocked by maraviroc, which prevents binding rather than fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: p17 is a structural matrix protein of the virion and is not the target of any antiretroviral class here.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with HIV infection is started on raltegravir. Which of the following steps of the retroviral life cycle does this drug block?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding of the virus to the CCR5 coreceptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Budding of assembled virions from the cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cleavage of polyproteins into mature units

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversion of viral RNA into viral DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insertion of viral DNA into the host genome

explanation.summary: Integrase strand transfer inhibitors block integration of newly made viral DNA into the host cell genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally, newly made viral DNA must be integrated into the host cell's genome, a step catalyzed by the enzyme integrase. Integrase strand transfer inhibitors such as raltegravir inhibit integrase and prevent this DNA from infecting cells. INSTIs are very common components of modern HIV regimens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding to CCR5 is blocked by maraviroc, an entry inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Budding is the final step blocked indirectly by protease inhibitors, not by integrase inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cleavage of polyproteins into mature viral units is blocked by protease inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conversion of RNA into DNA is blocked by NRTIs and NNRTIs acting on reverse transcriptase.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with HIV infection is started on darunavir. Which of the following best describes the effect of this drug on the virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Polyprotein chains are not cut into mature viral proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: The elongating nucleotide chain is terminated prematurely

choices.label: C
choices.text: The virus cannot bind the CCR5 receptor on the cell surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Viral DNA is not inserted into the host cell's own genome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral RNA is not converted into double-stranded viral DNA

explanation.summary: Protease inhibitors block the enzyme that cuts polyproteins into mature viral proteins, preventing formation of mature virions.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protease inhibitors act on the final step of replication, which involves budding of the virus from the host cell. Protease is the enzyme responsible for cutting polyprotein chains into the smaller proteins that make up mature HIV units. Inhibiting protease stops mature viral particles from forming, and these drugs are often considered when a patient is not responding to initial antiretroviral therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Premature chain termination describes the nucleoside analogues, which act at reverse transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Blocking CCR5 binding describes maraviroc, an entry inhibitor acting before the virus gets inside.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking insertion of viral DNA into the genome describes the integrase strand transfer inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocking conversion of RNA to DNA describes inhibition of reverse transcriptase by NRTIs and NNRTIs.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with HIV infection is prescribed atazanavir together with low-dose ritonavir. His clinician explains that the second drug is included specifically to raise the concentration of the first. Which of the following best explains this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes are induced

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatic cytochrome P450 metabolism is inhibited

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intestinal absorption of the first drug is increased

choices.label: D
choices.text: Renal tubular secretion of the first drug is blocked

choices.label: E
choices.text: The first drug is displaced from plasma proteins

explanation.summary: Ritonavir and cobicistat are pharmacokinetic enhancers that inhibit hepatic CYP450 to raise levels of the boosted drug.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protease inhibitors often require a booster with ritonavir, which is itself a protease inhibitor, or with cobicistat. These boosters inhibit hepatic cytochrome P450, increasing the concentration of the protease inhibitor. This lets the drug be given less frequently, improving adherence, and it also limits the adverse effects seen at higher doses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Induction of CYP450 would lower rather than raise the level of the boosted drug; efavirenz is the inducer discussed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Enhanced intestinal absorption is not the described mechanism of ritonavir or cobicistat.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick attributes boosting to CYP450 inhibition, not to blockade of renal elimination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Displacement from plasma proteins is not how these pharmacokinetic enhancers work.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A clinician wants to build an antiretroviral regimen that does not require a pharmacokinetic booster, because the patient is already taking several medications metabolized by cytochrome P450. Which of the following antiretrovirals is most likely to require such a booster and should therefore be avoided?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bictegravir

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dolutegravir

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elvitegravir

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raltegravir

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tenofovir

explanation.summary: Among the integrase inhibitors, elvitegravir is the one that commonly requires boosting.
explanation.whyCorrect: Only a handful of HIV medications require a pharmacokinetic enhancer. The most common ones that need boosters are the protease inhibitors atazanavir, darunavir, and lopinavir, and the integrase strand transfer inhibitor elvitegravir. Avoiding elvitegravir avoids the added CYP450 inhibition from ritonavir or cobicistat.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bictegravir is cleared by CYP450 but is not listed among the drugs that require boosting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dolutegravir is an integrase inhibitor that is not listed as requiring a booster.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Raltegravir is an integrase inhibitor but is not among the drugs listed as requiring a booster.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tenofovir is a nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitor and is not a boosted agent.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman taking a boosted protease inhibitor asks why an extra pill that has no direct antiviral benefit for her was added. Apart from raising the drug concentration, which of the following is the main clinical advantage of adding this agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It broadens the regimen's activity against resistant strains

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can be substituted for one of the two required NRTIs

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lowers the dosing frequency and improves adherence

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents mother-to-child transmission during pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: It removes the need for HLA-B*5701 genetic testing

explanation.summary: Boosting prolongs the duration of the drug so it can be taken less often, which improves adherence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ritonavir and cobicistat inhibit CYP enzymes, which prolongs the duration of the boosted drug and decreases how often the patient must take it. Less frequent dosing helps with adherence to the medication. Boosting also limits the adverse effects that would be seen if higher doses were used instead.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Boosters improve pharmacokinetics; they are not described as broadening activity against resistant virus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Boosters do not replace an NRTI; regimens still generally contain two NRTIs plus a third active drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reducing perinatal transmission comes from effective combination therapy during pregnancy, not from the booster itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HLA-B*5701 testing is required in all HIV-positive patients regardless of the regimen chosen.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 29-year-old treatment-naive woman is newly diagnosed with HIV infection and is ready to begin antiretroviral therapy. Which of the following combinations is most commonly used to initiate treatment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One nucleoside inhibitor plus one fusion inhibitor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Three nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two non-nucleoside inhibitors plus one protease inhibitor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two nucleoside inhibitors plus one integrase inhibitor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two protease inhibitors plus one non-nucleoside inhibitor

explanation.summary: Initial HIV therapy is generally two NRTIs plus a third drug from another class, most commonly an INSTI.
explanation.whyCorrect: A multidrug treatment plan best suppresses HIV RNA, and many studies support initiating therapy with two NRTIs plus one drug from another class, most commonly an integrase strand transfer inhibitor. In some cases the third drug may instead be a protease inhibitor or an NNRTI. This multidrug approach reduces morbidity and mortality related to the infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fusion and entry inhibitors are not typically first-line choices.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Three NRTIs is not the described initial approach; the third drug comes from a different class.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Regimens are built on two NRTIs, not on two NNRTIs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Two protease inhibitors is not a standard backbone; only a booster dose of ritonavir accompanies another PI.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man with HIV infection has been adherent to a three-drug regimen for two years. Which of the following best describes what this therapy is expected to accomplish?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete eradication of provirus from the host genome

choices.label: B
choices.text: Correction of the proofreading defect of reverse transcriptase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cure of the infection once the viral load is undetectable

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prevention of all resistance mutations for the patient's life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of HIV RNA that slows progression to AIDS

explanation.summary: Combination antiretroviral therapy suppresses HIV RNA and can slow or halt progression to AIDS, but it does not cure the infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Combination therapy is the mainstay of highly active antiretroviral treatment and can slow or halt progression to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. By suppressing viral RNA and reducing the inflammatory immune response, it keeps the CD4 count up. HIV remains incurable, which is why prevention is emphasized so heavily.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Integration of viral DNA into the host genome is one of the reasons HIV cannot be eradicated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lack of proofreading by reverse transcriptase is an intrinsic viral property that drugs do not repair.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An undetectable viral load reflects suppression, not cure; the virus is described as incurable but manageable.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Combination therapy raises the number of mutations needed for resistance but does not prevent all of them.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A student asks why a patient with HIV infection is never treated with a single antiretroviral agent. Which of the following provides the best explanation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A single agent cannot penetrate the central nervous system

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single agent is always more nephrotoxic than a combination

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antiretrovirals are inactive unless a booster is also given

choices.label: D
choices.text: Combination tablets are less expensive than single agents

choices.label: E
choices.text: More mutations are needed for resistance with several drugs

explanation.summary: Multiple drugs are used simultaneously so that the virus must acquire more mutations before it becomes resistant.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV has a high mutation rate because reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading, which lets the virus quickly adapt to treatment. Using several drugs at once increases the number of mutations the virus would need to escape therapy. These medications are therefore always used in combination, which helps reduce resistance rates.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Central nervous system penetration is not the reason given for combination therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nephrotoxicity is drug specific, such as with tenofovir DF or atazanavir, and is not a reason to combine drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Only a handful of antiretrovirals require a booster; most are fully active without one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Combination tablets are used to reduce pill burden and improve adherence, not because of cost.

questions.topicName: Antiretrovirals: Drugs to Treat and Prevent HIV Infection

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops fever, myalgia, and cough during influenza season. A rapid influenza test is positive, and she is started on oseltamivir. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of host receptor binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blockade of the M2 ion channel

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibition of viral DNA polymerase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of viral neuraminidase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibition of viral RNA polymerase

explanation.summary: Oseltamivir and zanamivir treat influenza by inhibiting the viral enzyme neuraminidase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neuraminidase inhibitors are the mainstay of influenza treatment, and oseltamivir is the current drug of choice. Neuraminidase is a viral enzyme that releases budding viruses from the infected cell's outer membrane, so blocking it reduces the rate at which newly formed virions reach healthy cells and slows the progression of infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neuraminidase inhibitors act at viral release, not at the receptor-binding step of entry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: M2 ion channel blockade is the mechanism of amantadine and rimantadine, not oseltamivir.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibition of viral DNA polymerase describes guanosine analogs such as acyclovir and ganciclovir.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Activity against viral RNA polymerase describes ribavirin, the agent used for RSV.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with influenza is treated with zanamivir. Which step of the viral life cycle is most directly interrupted by this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assembly of new virion particles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attachment to the host cell receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endocytosis of the virion into the cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of progeny virions from the cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replication of the viral genome

explanation.summary: Neuraminidase inhibitors act at the release-of-progeny-virus step of the influenza life cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neuraminidase frees budding virions from the outer membrane of the infected cell. Oseltamivir and zanamivir block that enzyme, so newly formed virus stays tethered to the cell it came from and fewer particles travel on to healthy cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Virion assembly proceeds normally; only the final release of the particles is blocked.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor binding occurs before the drug's target step and is unaffected by neuraminidase inhibition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endocytosis brings the virion into the cell and is not the step these drugs block.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genome replication is the target of nucleic acid synthesis inhibitors such as ribavirin.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with laboratory-confirmed influenza and asthma is seen 1 day after symptom onset. Which of the following is the current drug of choice for treating his influenza?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acyclovir

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amantadine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ganciclovir

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oseltamivir

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ribavirin

explanation.summary: Oseltamivir is the current drug of choice for influenza.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neuraminidase inhibitors are the mainstay of influenza management, and among them oseltamivir is the current drug of choice. Comorbid asthma also places this patient at increased risk of progressing to severe influenza, which supports treating him.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acyclovir is a guanosine analog used for HSV and VZV infections.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Amantadine is an M2 ion channel blocker formerly used for influenza but discontinued because of resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ganciclovir is a guanosine analog used for cytomegalovirus infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ribavirin is the drug used for RSV and hepatitis C, not for influenza.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman asks when influenza antiviral therapy must be started to be effective. Which of the following describes the window of maximum effectiveness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: After the fever has resolved

choices.label: B
choices.text: At any point during the illness

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only once hypoxemia develops

choices.label: D
choices.text: Within 48 hours of symptom onset

choices.label: E
choices.text: Within 7 days of symptom onset

explanation.summary: Influenza antivirals have maximum effectiveness when started within 48 hours of symptom onset.
explanation.whyCorrect: These drugs work best when given in the first 48 hours after symptoms begin. After that window, the drug does not provide any additional benefit, so the timing of the first dose is the single most important determinant of whether therapy helps.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Waiting for defervescence would push treatment past the window of benefit.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Timing is crucial; the drugs are not equally useful at any point in the illness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Waiting for hypoxemia would delay therapy well beyond the effective window.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Seven days is far outside the effective window; benefit is lost after 48 hours.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with influenza presents 4 days after symptom onset and asks why oseltamivir is unlikely to help him now. Which of the following best explains the loss of benefit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neutralizing antibody binds the drug and inactivates it after several days

choices.label: B
choices.text: Resistance mutations arise in nearly every strain by the fourth day

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drug is cleared too rapidly to reach the airway this late in illness

choices.label: D
choices.text: The virus switches to cell-to-cell spread that the drug cannot block

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral budding has slowed, so there is little neuraminidase activity left to block

explanation.summary: After 48 hours the rate of new virion budding is very low, so a neuraminidase inhibitor has little left to do.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oseltamivir works by keeping budding virions tethered to the infected cell's outer membrane. Past the 48-hour mark the rate of newly formed virus is very low, so blocking neuraminidase is essentially ineffective because the virus is no longer budding.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody does not inactivate oseltamivir, and this is not the reason for the 48-hour rule.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Resistance from mutations occurs in some strains, but most circulating strains remain susceptible.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Drug clearance does not change with the day of illness; the problem is the absence of the target activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The explanation for late failure is reduced budding, not a switch in the mode of viral spread.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with influenza is prescribed an antiviral given as an inhaled aerosol powder. Which of the following adverse effects is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute kidney injury

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hemolytic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nasal and airway irritation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral neuropathy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Photosensitivity rash

explanation.summary: Zanamivir is inhaled, and its adverse effects reflect that route: airway and nasal irritation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neuraminidase inhibitors are generally well tolerated, and their side effects track with the route of administration. Zanamivir is an inhaled aerosol powder and primarily causes airway irritation, along with headache, sore throat, and myalgia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acute kidney injury is not a reported adverse effect of zanamivir.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemolytic anemia is the black box adverse effect of ribavirin, not of an inhaled neuraminidase inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peripheral neuropathy is not among the reported adverse effects of these drugs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Photosensitivity is not an adverse effect associated with neuraminidase inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man takes an oral neuraminidase inhibitor for influenza and calls about a side effect. Which of the following is he most likely to report?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Airway irritation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hearing loss

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemolytic anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nausea and vomiting

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neutropenic fever

explanation.summary: Oseltamivir is given orally and mainly causes headache and gastrointestinal upset.
explanation.whyCorrect: Adverse effects of neuraminidase inhibitors follow their route of administration. Because oseltamivir is swallowed, it mainly produces gastrointestinal disturbance such as nausea and vomiting, along with headache.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Airway irritation is characteristic of inhaled zanamivir rather than oral oseltamivir.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hearing loss is not an adverse effect associated with these antiviral agents.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemolytic anemia is an adverse effect of ribavirin, which is used for RSV and hepatitis C.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutropenia is reported with ribavirin therapy, not with oral neuraminidase inhibitors.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: A 58-year-old lung transplant recipient with severe RSV infection is given ribavirin. Which of the following best describes how this drug works?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocks the M2 ion channel and prevents viral uncoating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocks viral attachment to host sialic acid receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits guanine nucleotide synthesis and halts strand elongation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits viral neuraminidase and blocks virion release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits viral protease and prevents polyprotein cleavage

explanation.summary: Ribavirin is a guanine nucleotide synthesis inhibitor that mimics purine structure and stops viral nucleic acid elongation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ribavirin is a broad-spectrum nucleoside antiviral that mimics purine structure. It competitively inhibits nucleic acid synthesis by being incorporated into the growing nucleic acid strand and halting elongation, which decreases viral replication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: M2 channel blockade describes amantadine and rimantadine, which are no longer used for influenza.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ribavirin acts inside the cell on nucleic acid synthesis, not at the attachment step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neuraminidase inhibition describes oseltamivir and zanamivir, which are used for influenza.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Protease inhibition is not the mechanism of ribavirin as described for RSV therapy.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: Five patients with respiratory syncytial virus infection are evaluated. Which of the following patients is the most appropriate candidate for antiviral therapy with ribavirin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 30-year-old with a mild RSV upper respiratory infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 70-year-old with treated hypertension and an RSV cough

choices.label: C
choices.text: A bone marrow transplant recipient with severe RSV pneumonia

choices.label: D
choices.text: A healthy 2-year-old with RSV bronchiolitis and a good appetite

choices.label: E
choices.text: A woman in the third trimester of pregnancy with RSV

explanation.summary: Ribavirin for RSV is reserved for severely immunocompromised patients, such as transplant recipients.
explanation.whyCorrect: RSV is usually self-limiting and managed supportively. Antiviral therapy with ribavirin is only indicated in patients who are severely immunocompromised, such as transplant patients or those with certain cancers, and even then it must be considered carefully and individualized because of the drug's risks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mild RSV upper respiratory illness is self-limiting and requires no antiviral therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Well-controlled hypertension does not make a patient severely immunocompromised.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A healthy toddler with bronchiolitis is managed with supportive care, not ribavirin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ribavirin is an FDA category X drug and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: A previously healthy 9-month-old infant has rhinorrhea, cough, and low-grade fever from RSV. He is feeding well and has normal oxygen saturation. Which of the following is the preferred management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acyclovir

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oseltamivir

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ribavirin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supportive care alone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zanamivir

explanation.summary: The preferred treatment of RSV infection is no antiviral treatment, because the infection is self-limiting.
explanation.whyCorrect: RSV is a self-limiting infection, so the preferred approach is supportive care: maintaining oxygenation, replenishing fluids, and managing symptoms. Antiviral therapy is reserved for severely immunocompromised patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acyclovir is a guanosine analog used for HSV and VZV infections.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oseltamivir treats influenza and has no activity against RSV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ribavirin is restricted to severely immunocompromised patients because of its risks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zanamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor for influenza, not an RSV drug.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with known asthma has an RSV lower respiratory tract infection with cough and diffuse wheezing. Which of the following is most likely to relieve his symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aerosolized ribavirin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bronchodilators and steroids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous antibiotics

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral amantadine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral oseltamivir

explanation.summary: In RSV lower respiratory tract infection with cough and wheezing, bronchodilators and steroids may relieve symptoms, especially with underlying reactive airway disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Management of RSV is supportive. In patients with lower respiratory tract infection who present with cough and wheezing, bronchodilators and steroids may result in symptom relief, particularly when the patient has underlying reactive airway disease such as asthma or COPD.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ribavirin is reserved for severely immunocompromised patients with RSV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibiotics do not treat a viral lower respiratory tract infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amantadine was an influenza drug and is no longer used because of resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oseltamivir is an influenza drug and has no role in RSV infection.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman is counseled before starting ribavirin. Which of the following adverse effects carries an FDA black box warning for this drug?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemolytic anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatic failure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nephrotoxicity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stevens-Johnson syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Torsades de pointes

explanation.summary: Hemolytic anemia is the black box warning issued by the FDA for ribavirin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ribavirin is associated with anemia, hemolytic anemia, and neutropenia. The hemolytic anemia is serious enough that it carries an FDA black box warning, because the resulting anemia can worsen preexisting cardiac disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatic failure is not the black box warning attached to ribavirin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nephrotoxicity is not the warned-about toxicity for this drug.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is not a described ribavirin adverse effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Torsades de pointes is not among ribavirin's reported adverse effects.

questions.topicName: Antivirals 2 of 2: Drugs to Treat Influenza Virus and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection
